Missing evidence matters when it could change a decision.

Report an error

These measurement priorities link evidence gaps to specific decision questions. They do not rank national priorities or use a hidden score. Each item states the decision affected, what evidence is missing, the feasibility and sensitivity constraints, and what would become knowable if that evidence existed. Priority labels describe sequencing within this resource; they are not government, funding or policy rankings.

How to read itWhat a measurement priority does not establishWhat remains uncertain about the priorities themselvesVerifyMeasurements that would change decisionsMore evidence
01What it means

How to read the priorities

A measurement item is an evidence-to-decision record, not a recommendation to government or a wish list. It identifies the pages and decisions affected, the evidence currently missing, feasibility and sensitivity constraints, the basis for its position in this resource’s measurement priorities, and what would change if the evidence became available.

02Evidence

Stable references for citation

Each priority has a stable reference, such as MA-001, so that it can be cited, linked and corrected without depending on a title that may change.

03Analysis

Priority labels describe evidence sequencing

This resource does not compress decision importance, feasibility, evidence quality and sensitivity into one opaque score. P0/P1 indicate how directly a missing measure blocks questions covered by this resource and how it depends on other evidence. They are not national policy priorities, funding rankings or judgements about the importance of the underlying population or issue.

04System context

Why measurement is part of this resource

Measurement connects the rest of this resource. A new round of a population survey can update People and test whether infrastructure changes reached users. A verified access-point register can connect Providers to Access. Post-reform use and complaints data can connect Reforms and Payments to service quality. A firm-finance journey can connect business constraints to actual applications, approvals, terms and outcomes.

What this does not establish

What a measurement priority does not establish

A P0/P1 label does not mean the unmeasured phenomenon is large, worsening or absent. It describes only how the evidence gap affects the questions covered by this resource. A measurement gap is not a zero, and an unmeasured outcome is not evidence that a reform failed.

What we still do not know

What remains uncertain about the priorities themselves

Feasibility, sensitivity and cost can change when a specific measurement is designed with the institution that would collect or hold the data. Those implementation facts cannot be assumed in advance and would need to be confirmed before any commissioning decision.

07Measurement update

How the priorities change

When a measurement is completed, the new evidence is assessed against the decision it was meant to improve. If the question becomes answerable, the gap closes or narrows; if a new incompatibility or uncertainty appears, the item is revised while keeping the same reference so its history remains traceable.

08Verify the evidence

Verify each gap

Open any measurement item to see what is known now, what evidence is still missing, which pages and decisions are affected, how feasible the measurement appears, what sensitivity constraints apply, how its priority label was assigned, and which evidence records revealed the gap.

Measurement priorities

Measurements that would change decisions

Each measurement priority sets out the current evidence, the missing evidence, what the decision would gain, the proposed method, feasibility, sensitivity or data-responsibility constraints, the priority rationale and what would change if the evidence became available.

Measurement priorityP0 · People

A current people-side inclusion baseline

Current evidence: The Global Findex 2025 edition contains 2024 observations for many economies, but Yemen's latest representative account-ownership observation remains 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed, for 2022 (from the Yemen Findex 2021 study fielded in 2022–2023). Major payment-system and reform changes are more recent. The World Bank publishes 2021-wave values for domestic remittances: 17.7% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed sent them and 31.9% received them, also by group (shown on the People page); the channels through which the money moved are not shown. Adding a finance module to an existing survey is one route to such a baseline. The Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2022–2023 of the Central Statistical Organization and UNICEF was designed for all 22 governorates (41 enumeration areas could not be visited) and asks one household question on finance, whether any member has a bank account, which its findings report does not tabulate. The World Bank's mobile phone survey of August–September 2022 interviewed 1,297 adults aged 18 and over with mobile phones and records each respondent's area of control, the internationally recognized government or the de facto authorities. For shop credit to households (customers buying from shops on credit) there are local observations, not a baseline: in a 2024 Cash Consortium of Yemen study, 11 of 21 business owners who answered in Ad-Dali and 10 of 21 in Ja’ar said that fewer customers bought on credit when cash assistance was distributed.

Decision it would strengthen: A current population measure would allow change since the previous wave to be assessed without projecting reform results onto the population.

Reference MA-001
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: account ownership, use, saving, borrowing, payments, resilience, gender, income, age, rurality, household remittance receipt, remittance channel, remittance currency, remittance frequency, financial capability, collateral, shop or supplier credit, mobile-money account

Missing evidence: New representative Yemen demand-side survey or equivalent approved microdata with weights and clear coverage, including remittance receipt, channel and frequency.

Questions it would answer:

  • Whether account ownership and use have changed since the latest representative people-side wave.
  • Which population groups now have lower/higher access and use under a current sampling frame.
  • Whether recent payment/reform changes coincide with measured population change without inferring causality.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: A current population-level inclusion baseline comparable on core concepts with the latest available wave.

Measurement guardrail
The latest representative people-side measure predates the current reform and infrastructure changes. A new measurement must document its population, geographic coverage, fieldwork period and survey weights, and keep core concepts comparable with the previous wave. The World Bank publishes no mobile-money-account figure for Yemen's 2021 study, and its figure for an account at a financial institution is the same as its account figure: if a new survey publishes mobile-money values, part of any rise in account ownership may come from the wider measure, not from real change, so the two definitions must be reported separately.
Feasibility
MEDIUM — requires a representative demand-side survey or approved weighted microdata collection.
Why this is a priority
P0 among these measurement priorities because multiple current policy/product questions depend on population outcomes while newer evidence is largely administrative, institutional or programme-based.
What the measurement would change
This resource could update the people-side baseline, assess change by comparable dimensions, and stop relying on an older population wave for current decisions.
Measurement priorityP0 · Payments / People

Active and repeat digital use

Current evidence: Administrative data show registrations, infrastructure and transactions, while historical evidence also records dormancy and one-time or imposed use; unique repeat users are not measured consistently.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use.

Reference MA-002
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: unique user, frequency, recency, value, duration, merchant use, cash-out, dormancy

Missing evidence: Administrative data from providers or payment systems, with deduplication rules, and/or demand-side active-use measures.

Questions it would answer:

  • Whether digital finance is repeat use rather than registration or one-off activity.
  • Which channels/providers are associated with sustained use.
  • How much administrative activity can be interpreted as durable financial use.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: Deduplicated active-user and repeat-use evidence over time.

Trace the evidence Accounts and transactions are not unique people · Wallet and subscriber counts from different publications are not yet reconciled · 807,919 accounts did not mean 807,919 active people · Most recorded 2019 e-money value still revolved around cash and account transfers · What does the payment system actually count?

Measurement guardrail
Registered accounts, subscribers, terminals or transaction totals cannot stand in for unique active people. Frequency, recency, value and duration of use should be tracked where feasible.
Feasibility
MEDIUM — possible through provider or payment-system data if definitions and deduplication rules are agreed; may need demand-side validation.
Why this is a priority
P0 among these measurement priorities because digital infrastructure and transaction evidence are expanding while unique repeat use remains unresolved.
What the measurement would change
Separates registration and transaction volume from sustained user adoption.
Measurement priorityP0 · People / Equity

Financial inclusion across population groups: measure disparities before explaining them

Current evidence: Within the same survey wave, account ownership differs by 12.9 percentage points between women (5.4%) and men (18.3%), by 9.0 percentage points between adults in the poorest 40% (6.5%) and the richest 60% (15.5%) by household income, and by 11.1 percentage points between adults aged 15–24 (5.0%) and those aged 25 and over (16.1%). Comparable current differences by finer age groups and by displacement status are not established in the evidence base, and the contribution of identity, device, income, geography, trust and household constraints to any measured disparity is not established.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show which subgroup differences are actually measured and would allow plausible mechanisms to be tested without treating untested explanations as causes.

Reference MA-003
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: sex/gender, age group, displacement status, access, use, quality, identity, device, income, work, geography, trust, household constraints, administrative-area coverage (both areas of control), digital literacy

Missing evidence: Representative or clearly bounded disaggregated quantitative evidence to measure subgroup outcomes, with linked mechanism variables and qualitative or stronger causal designs where explanation is required.

Questions it would answer:

  • Which differences in access, use and quality are actually measured by sex/gender, age group and displacement status under comparable designs.
  • Which measured differences are associated with device, income, geography, identity, trust or household constraints.
  • Which candidate interventions could be tested against observed frictions without presuming a cause.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: Current subgroup estimates with clear universes and comparable definitions, plus mechanism-aware evidence able to distinguish association from explanation.

Trace the evidence A measured gender gap in account ownership · Account ownership and measured gaps: Global Findex 2021 wave (Yemen fieldwork 2022–23)

Measurement guardrail
Do not turn an unmeasured subgroup into a measured gap. Measuring a disparity and explaining it are separate evidence products; causal mechanisms require a design capable of testing them.
Feasibility
MEDIUM — survey modules and bounded qualitative work are feasible, but causal attribution needs stronger designs.
Why this is a priority
P0 among these measurement priorities because material disparities by sex, household income and age are measured within one survey wave, while current evidence for finer age groups and by displacement status, and causal explanations, remain incomplete; without new measurement, unmeasured subgroup gaps and their causes would remain speculative.
What the measurement would change
Keeps apart what needs different evidence: whether a disparity is measured, what is associated with it, and what design could test a causal mechanism or intervention.
Measurement priorityP0 · Firms / MSME

A current MSME finance demand/use baseline

Current evidence: The 2022 Yemen Enterprise Survey (formal firms in seven governorates) and programme evidence from the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) can each be used within its own scope, and the Yemen Loan Guarantee Program's reports count guarantees issued, not firms; none of them supplies a current representative national MSME finance baseline. For collateral and terms the evidence is historical: an evaluation of IFAD-financed rural credit in Yemen from 1993 to 2010 by IFAD's Independent Office of Evaluation reports collateral requirements, high transaction costs and long approval procedures among the reasons poor households were said to avoid the partner bank's credit, in specific project areas before the conflict.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show the finance journey from need and application through approval or rejection, terms, use and repayment pressure, while SMEPS remains a separate programme-evidence layer.

Reference MA-004
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: finance need, application, approval, rejection, collateral, terms, informal finance, digital payments, gender, size, sector, geography

Missing evidence: A representative survey of firms/MSMEs, or validated administrative data linked to firm-level data, with explicit definitions, covering finance need, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and outcome; and unique-firm identification across programme registers, and whether guaranteed loans add to lending (additionality).

Questions it would answer:

  • How many firms need finance, apply, are approved/rejected and on what terms.
  • Which firm types and locations face the largest financing frictions.
  • Where the finance journey shows the largest measured frictions.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: A current national firm-finance journey with explicit sampling frame and stage-by-stage bases.

Measurement guardrail
The 2013 and 2022 surveys use incompatible sampling frames; do not build a trend between them unless comparability is established variable by variable. SMEPS's own 2024 report adds a programme KPI (19% of supported MSMEs accessed financial services), but this does not replace a current representative MSME demand/use baseline, and the base on which this KPI is calculated is not yet clearly documented.
Feasibility
MEDIUM — requires a representative firm/MSME survey and/or validated administrative-firm linkage.
Why this is a priority
P0 among these measurement priorities because the current 2022 seven-governorate survey and SMEPS programme evidence answer different bounded questions and cannot supply a national baseline.
What the measurement would change
This resource could quantify attrition from finance need through application, approval/rejection, amount/terms, use and repayment pressure nationally.
Measurement priorityP0 · Providers / Geography

A register of active financial access points

Current evidence: Current official rosters establish selected listing, licensing and event states, but do not provide a complete, geocoded register of active branches, agents, merchants and other service points. The IMF Financial Access Survey, as published in the World Bank's World Development Indicators (series FB.ATM.TOTL.P5, FB.CBK.BRCH.P5 and FB.CBK.DPTR.P3), last reports Yemen for 2015: 5.81 ATMs and 1.5 commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults, and 103.1 depositors with commercial banks per 1,000 adults. The series stops in 2015 and its population denominators are the IMF's; the values are dated historical context, not a current measure of access to, or use of, financial services. Local observations point to a liquidity dimension that registers do not capture: a May 2026 Cash Consortium of Yemen report, in its section on humanitarian multi-purpose cash assistance, records agents lacking enough cash during the Ramadan and Eid holiday period, with waits of four to five hours (from one interview with a programme manager), and funds released only in denominations of YER 100 and 200. The series behind SDG indicator 8.10.1 (commercial bank branches and automated teller machines relative to the adult population, from the IMF Financial Access Survey as published in World Development Indicators) hold no Yemen value after 2015 (in the series as published on 8 October 2026); the 2015 values appear only as dated history, and missing is not zero.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish listing and licensing from operation and observed access before any access or opportunity map is interpreted.

Reference MA-005
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: branch, ATM, agent, merchant, exchanger, wallet point, status, service, coordinates, hours, liquidity, microfinance provider panel, reporting scope, exchanger flows, agent and till liquidity, banknote denominations, withdrawal caps

Missing evidence: An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated.

Questions it would answer:

  • Where operating financial access points are actually available.
  • Which populations/areas face longer travel or thinner channel coverage.
  • Which listed/licensed locations cannot yet be verified as operating.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: A current register of operating access points, dated by source and subject to documented disclosure rules.

Listed/licensed address is not necessarily active access; modelled accessibility must remain distinct from observed service use.
Feasibility
MEDIUM-HIGH if regulator/providers can supply point-level status and location under a shared governance rule.
Why this is a priority
P0 among these measurement priorities because access decisions and atlas design are blocked by the difference between institutional lists and verified operating presence.
What the measurement would change

Measurement priorityP0 · Consumer protection / Quality

Consumer experience and redress outcomes

Current evidence: The 2023 Instructions of CBY-Aden set out the complaint path and its time limits. They require the providers they cover to report to the central bank's consumer-protection department every three months on the complaints they have handled, by nature and type, with the measures taken (p.7), and provide for the central bank to prepare and publish annual reports of aggregate complaint information (p.31). No such report was located on cby-ye.com (its news items, publications and rules pages, and its 2024 and 2025 annual reports, checked on 11 October 2026). A duty to report or publish does not show that the data exist publicly or that providers comply; actual complaint volumes, resolution times and outcomes are not documented in the available evidence.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would allow redress performance and service quality to be assessed rather than inferred from the existence of rules.

Reference MA-006
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: complaint volume, type, channel, resolution time, outcome, repeat issue, fees, disclosure, trust

Missing evidence: Complaint and redress data from providers and the regulator, plus consumer-side evidence on experience, including fees, disclosure and trust.

Questions it would answer:

  • Whether complaint channels are used and resolved within expected time.
  • Where redress fails or delays occur.
  • Whether consumer-protection architecture translates into practical remedy.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: Complaint volumes, resolution times/outcomes and user experience linked to the documented redress process.

Trace the evidence Consumer protection and complaint path: official rules and guidance · The complaint path is documented; there is no evidence yet on how it performs · If a complaint is not resolved, what happens?

Measurement priorityP0 · Social protection / Payments

Persistence of financial use after cash transfers

Current evidence: Programme evidence can establish delivery, beneficiary reach, successful payout and exposure to an account or wallet; sustained use after the transfer remains unmeasured. An existing instrument records respondents in both areas of control: the World Bank's mobile phone survey of August–September 2022 records each respondent's area of control and asks respondents to rank their three most important sources of income; a later round could add questions on how transfers are received and used. UNICEF's releases on the World Bank-funded unconditional cash transfer give its announced reach, not confirmed payments, and its channels in the 18th payment cycle, to mid-October 2024 (payment sites, mobile teams and home outreach, and an e-wallet pilot), and announce that the 19th cycle, from 11 December 2024, would end the programme in its then-current form. A May 2026 report on humanitarian multi-purpose cash assistance, a different programme, records from one interview agents short of cash at cash-out during the Ramadan and Eid holiday period.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show whether transfer-related financial exposure becomes persistent use and which observed conditions are associated with repeat use.

Reference MA-009
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: payment receipt, account/wallet exposure, activation, repeat use, merchant use, saving, cash-out, time since transfer, cash-out constraints

Missing evidence: Longitudinal programme or provider cohort data, or repeated beneficiary follow-up, with privacy-safe linkage from transfer receipt to account or wallet activation, repeat use, merchant use, saving and cash-out.

Questions it would answer:

  • Whether use of the account or wallet linked to the transfer continues after payout.
  • Which observed programme/provider conditions are associated with repeat use, merchant use or saving.
  • Whether the evidence supports only payout-related exposure or continued use after payout.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: Privacy-safe longitudinal or repeated follow-up evidence after transfer receipt.

Measurement priorityP0 · Reforms / Payments / Quality

Reform transmission and service quality

Current evidence: Recent evidence documents rules, institutions, projects, procurement and selected infrastructure activity, but the chain to access, use, quality and outcomes is incomplete.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show the furthest evidenced state of each reform and the next unmeasured result without treating missing evidence as failure.

Reference MA-010
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: rule, go-live, participant coverage, availability, latency, failure, cost, access, use, complaints, outcome

Missing evidence: Reform-specific operational and user-side evidence tied to the same implementation timeline, from go-live through coverage, reliability, cost and outcome.

Questions it would answer:

  • Which state each reform has actually reached.
  • Where the transmission chain stops being evidenced.
  • What next operational/user indicator should be measured.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: Reform-specific operational, access, use, quality and outcome indicators aligned to implementation dates.

Measurement guardrail
Every transition from infrastructure to outcome requires its own indicator; missing downstream evidence is not failure.
Feasibility
MEDIUM — depends on access to the institutions implementing each reform and on indicator definitions.
Why this is a priority
P0 among these measurement priorities because rules, institutions and projects are current while downstream results remain unevenly measured.
What the measurement would change
Allows this resource to say how far a reform has progressed in evidence terms without equating milestones with outcomes.
Measurement priorityP1 · Identity / Digital access

Digital onboarding and identity journeys

Current evidence: CBY-Aden's e-money rules and its electronic know-your-customer (KYC) instructions, which ask providers to report the average time to open or activate an account, are documented, but this resource lacks journey-level evidence on attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would identify where users leave or fail the onboarding journey and which frictions are associated with those points.

Reference MA-007
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: ID possession, KYC attempt, completion, rejection, reason, device/SIM, eKYC, time/cost, provider

Missing evidence: Journey-level administrative or survey data across onboarding stages: identity and KYC verification, attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.

Questions it would answer:

  • Where users abandon onboarding.
  • Which identity/KYC steps create time/cost/rejection frictions.
  • Which candidate remedies could be tested against the observed frictions.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: Stage-level onboarding attempts, completion, rejection/abandonment, time and cost.

Trace the evidence E-money rules set limits; they do not measure use · Layers of mobile e-money rules

Measurement guardrail
Do not infer exclusion from the existence of KYC rules; measure where and why people fail or abandon the journey.
Feasibility
MEDIUM — provider journey logs or structured user research.
Why this is a priority
P1 among these measurement priorities because rules are known but journey frictions remain unmeasured; important once higher-order baseline/use gaps are addressed.
What the measurement would change
Turns a generic KYC/exclusion debate into identifiable journey failure points.
Measurement priorityP1 · Credit infrastructure / MSME

Credit-infrastructure reach and actual use

Current evidence: CBY-Aden's published credit-information rules (exposure reporting on a set form and an enquiry before lending) and its launch of a defaulters registry show that credit-information infrastructure exists; lender participation, inquiry use and borrower reach are not yet documented as one complete evidence chain. This resource holds no current measure of the reach or use of credit infrastructure in Yemen. The most recent published measure of credit-registry coverage that this resource holds, the World Bank's Doing Business 2020 (data collected to May 2019; city covered: Sana'a; series since discontinued), is given with the defaulters registry's launch in the chronology; it is a historical reference, not a baseline for the registry CBY-Aden launched in 2026.

Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show whether credit infrastructure enters actual lending decisions, for which lenders and borrower groups.

Reference MA-008
More about this priority

Dimensions it would cover: credit bureau coverage, inquiries, report use, collateral registration, lender participation, borrower type, decision use, insolvency

Missing evidence: Administrative data from credit-information and collateral infrastructure and participating institutions on coverage, inquiries, report use, collateral registration, lender participation and borrower type.

Questions it would answer:

  • Whether lenders actually use credit-information/collateral infrastructure.
  • Which borrower groups enter the infrastructure.
  • How credit-information or collateral infrastructure is used within lending decision processes.

Evidence that cannot be produced without it: Operational participation, inquiry/use and borrower-coverage data tied to the infrastructure.

Evidence records that revealed these gaps

When was it measured or observed?The official 2026 roster (issue date not stated); 2026 enforcement decisions are separate evidence.
The official 2026 exchange and remittance roster can be counted; whether providers operate now is a separate question
The official 2026 roster of exchange and remittance providers issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 100 exchange companies, 231 individual exchange establishments and 111 remittance agents. These are roster entries counted by the roster's own classes: the three class totals are not a count of unique providers, nor a verified count of providers operating now. Because the roster does not state its issue date, CBY-Aden's 2026 decisions (dated January to September 2026) suspending or withdrawing the licences of named entities, or closing their premises, would have to be matched with the roster entity by entity, since a decision may or may not already be reflected in it; that matching has not been done.
Who or what does it apply to? Source-listed exchange companies, individual exchange establishments and remittance agents; entries are counted separately by the three classes used in the official roster.
Does not establish: Adding the three classes does not give a count of unique providers, because no rule for identifying the same entity across classes has been applied. Inclusion in the annual roster is not proof of current operation, branch activity or service availability, including for entities named in 2026 enforcement decisions. Why the numbers differ: the 2025 roster (record CLM-016) listed fewer entries in each of its three classes. The higher 2026 entries cannot be read as new providers entering the market: both rosters count entries by class rather than unique firms, this evidence base has not compared the two rosters entry by entry, and the 2026 roster states no issue date.
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?World Bank reporting year 2022; Global Findex 2021 study; Yemen fieldwork November 2022 to January 2023
Demand-side panel: 16 of its 32 measures have World Bank published values for Yemen
A 32-measure demand-side panel has been specified across access, barriers, digital use, saving, borrowing, resilience, remittances, income flows, financial worry and connectivity. Sixteen of its measures have values that the World Bank publishes for Yemen in the 2021 wave: an account (11.9% of adults) and an account at a financial institution (11.9%); saving any money (21.6%) and saving at a financial institution (3.1%); borrowing any money (51.3%), from a financial institution (1.8%) and from family or friends (41.1%); saying that emergency funds within 30 days would not be possible, or not knowing or not answering (10.8%; the other three answers are in the emergency-funds table on /people/); sending (17.7%), receiving (31.9%) or either sending or receiving (37.8%) domestic remittances; receiving wages (12.4%), a government transfer (3.8%) or payments for agricultural sales (28.9%); making or receiving a digital payment (9.3%); and making a digital merchant payment (0.6%). Of the other 16, two are mobile-money measures with no valid answer in the World Bank's public data for the study and no published value, and 14 have no World Bank published value for Yemen.
Who or what does it apply to? A pre-specified 32-measure panel: 16 measures with World Bank published values for Yemen; 14 measures the survey asked but for which the World Bank publishes no Yemen value, so that a value would require computation from licensed respondent-level data; and two mobile-money measures with no valid answer in the World Bank's public data for the study and no published value.
Does not establish: Of the 32 specified measures, 14 have no World Bank published value for Yemen in this wave and this resource does not compute them from respondent-level data, so they are planned, not measured; two (using and saving with a mobile-money account) have no valid answer in the World Bank's public data for the study and no published value, so no value exists for this wave.
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?As of the current governed edition of this resource
What we still do not know
The evidence gaps recorded in this resource as of the current governed edition of this resource are of these types: a missing period, a missing calculation base, a missing primary file, a map layer that cannot yet be built, and an unresolved source scope. A gap can close when new evidence arrives; a blank or missing observation is not zero and is not evidence of absence.
Who or what does it apply to? Documented gaps that block an answer: missing periods, unavailable sources, missing calculation bases and primary files not yet available
Does not establish: A gap is not zero, and it is not evidence of absence or failure.
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?2015, the last year reported for Yemen
ATMs, bank branches and depositors: Yemen's last values from the IMF Financial Access Survey in the World Development Indicators (2015)
The IMF Financial Access Survey, as published in the World Bank's World Development Indicators, last reports Yemen for 2015: 5.81 automated teller machines (ATMs) and 1.5 commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults, and 103.1 depositors with commercial banks per 1,000 adults. The series stop in 2015; these are dated historical values, not a current measure of access to, or use of, financial services.
Who or what does it apply to? Adults in Yemen, with the population denominators the IMF uses for the Financial Access Survey; branches and depositors of commercial banks only.
Does not establish: The values describe 2015, not access today, and count machines, branches and depositors, not the people who use them or where those points are.
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?Fieldwork July–September 2022 (Aden hub) and January–May 2023 (Sana'a hub)
MICS 2022–2023: one household question on bank accounts, not tabulated in its findings report
The Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2022–2023, carried out by the Central Statistical Organization with technical and financial support from UNICEF, was designed to give estimates for the 22 governorates of Yemen; 41 of the 880 selected enumeration areas could not be visited for security and safety reasons. Its household questionnaire asks one question on financial accounts, whether any member of the household has a bank account (item HC19), and its survey findings report does not tabulate the answers.
Who or what does it apply to? Households in the governorates covered by the survey design, apart from the enumeration areas that could not be visited.
Does not establish: The survey does not measure individual account ownership, account use, mobile money, saving or borrowing, and its findings report gives no result for the bank-account item.
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?August–September 2022 (Round I)
The World Bank's phone survey of August–September 2022 records respondents in both areas of control
The World Bank's Mobile Phone Survey Monitoring, Round I, interviewed 1,297 adult Yemenis aged 18 and over with mobile phones in August–September 2022, from a probability sample targeted across 21 governorates. It records each respondent's area of control, coded in the catalogue as the internationally recognized government or 'DFA', which this resource reads as the de facto authorities (the catalogue does not expand the abbreviation), and asks respondents to rank the three most important sources of income.
Who or what does it apply to? Adult Yemenis aged 18 and over with mobile phones, from a probability sample targeted across 21 governorates; the catalogue reports a response rate of around 28 percent.
Does not establish: Adults with mobile phones are not all adults; with a response rate of around 28 percent, and some governorate quotas not achieved, respondents may not represent all adults with mobile phones; the catalogue's sampling text names 18 governorates while its abstract says 21.
Open evidence record
